tags: Maternal death review and obstetric near miss

sections.section_title: Maternal death review and obstetric near miss

blocks.text: Clinical governance • Maternal safety • Audit and quality improvement
You are a doctor working in the obstetric unit. A woman has died following a postpartum haemorrhage, and the hospital has scheduled a maternal death review meeting.

items.text: Explain the purpose of a maternal death review.
Describe how you would review the case.
Identify possible avoidable factors and delays.
Explain the difference between a maternal death and an obstetric near-miss.
Discuss confidentiality, documentation and recommendations for preventing future deaths.

blocks.text: This station assesses your clinical knowledge, professionalism, communication, audit skills and ability to identify opportunities to improve patient safety.

A maternal death is the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of the duration and site of pregnancy, from a cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management, but not from accidental or incidental causes.
A death resulting from obstetric complications of pregnancy, labour or the puerperium, or from interventions, omissions, incorrect treatment or a chain of events resulting from these.

items.text: Postpartum haemorrhage.
Eclampsia.
Obstetric sepsis.
Uterine rupture.
Complications of unsafe abortion.
Amniotic fluid embolism.

blocks.text: A death resulting from a pre-existing disease or a disease that developed during pregnancy that was not directly due to obstetric causes but was aggravated by the physiological effects of pregnancy.

items.text: Cardiac disease worsened by pregnancy.
Severe sickle cell complications aggravated by pregnancy.
Severe malaria complicating pregnancy.
Certain respiratory or neurological diseases aggravated by pregnancy.

blocks.text: The death of a woman from direct or indirect obstetric causes more than 42 days but less than one year after the end of pregnancy.
This is distinguished from the standard maternal death definition, which uses the 42-day period.
An obstetric near-miss occurs when a woman nearly dies but survives a complication that occurred during pregnancy, childbirth or within 42 days of the end of pregnancy.

blocks.title: Examples include a woman who survives:

items.text: Severe postpartum haemorrhage requiring massive transfusion.
Eclampsia with critical complications.
Septic shock.
Uterine rupture.
Severe organ dysfunction requiring intensive care.

blocks.text: The WHO near-miss approach focuses on women who develop life-threatening complications and survive.

subsections.subsection_title: 3. Maternal death review versus maternal death audit

blocks.text: These terms overlap in practice, but it is useful to distinguish them in an OSCE.

rows: Systematic examination of the circumstances surrounding a maternal death to understand what happened and why
A structured assessment of care against accepted standards to identify deficiencies and corrective actions
A review process that gathers and analyses information about maternal deaths, often across multiple cases, to identify wider patterns and lessons
Review of a woman who survived a life-threatening obstetric complication
Comparison of clinical practice against agreed standards, followed by improvement and re-audit

blocks.text: The central principle is learning and prevention, not blame.

subsections.subsection_title: 4. Objectives of a maternal death review

blocks.title: State the following to the examiner:

items.text: Establish the cause and circumstances of death.
Identify avoidable factors and delays.
Assess the quality and timeliness of care.
Determine whether clinical guidelines were followed.
Identify system failures, resource gaps and communication problems.
Recommend practical corrective measures.
Assign responsibility for implementing those measures.
Monitor whether the changes reduce future maternal morbidity and mortality.

blocks.text: A review should not merely conclude that a woman died from haemorrhage or sepsis. It should establish what contributed to the deterioration and whether earlier recognition or better care might have changed the outcome.

subsections.subsection_title: 5. How to conduct a maternal death review

items.text: Confirm and notify the death

blocks.text: Follow the facility's reporting procedure and applicable national requirements. Notify the appropriate clinical leadership and maternal mortality review team.

items.text: Collect relevant information

blocks.text: Review the antenatal record, referral notes, labour monitoring chart, partograph where applicable, drug charts, observations, laboratory results, operative notes, blood bank records, resuscitation records and death documentation.

items.text: Construct a chronological timeline

blocks.text: Record when symptoms began, when the woman arrived, when assessments occurred, when deterioration was recognised, when treatment started, when senior help was requested and when definitive intervention occurred.

items.text: Determine the cause of death

blocks.text: Identify the underlying cause, the immediate cause and any contributing conditions. Distinguish confirmed facts from uncertain or unverified information.

items.text: Assess the care provided

blocks.text: Compare the clinical decisions and interventions with accepted standards and the resources available at the time.

items.text: Identify contributing factors

blocks.text: Consider patient-related, community, transport, referral, staffing, equipment, communication and clinical-management factors.

items.text: Agree on corrective actions

blocks.text: Recommend specific interventions with a named lead, deadline, measurable outcome and process for follow-up.

items.text: Implement and re-evaluate

blocks.text: Track completion of recommendations, repeat audits where appropriate and assess whether care has improved.
This is one of the most important frameworks for maternal mortality discussions, particularly in resource-limited settings.
The woman or family delays recognising danger or deciding to seek medical assistance.
Examples

items.text: Poor recognition of danger signs.
Financial barriers.
Fear, stigma or cultural barriers.
Family decision-making delays.
Previous negative experiences with healthcare.

blocks.text: The woman has decided to seek help but cannot reach an appropriate facility promptly.
Examples

items.text: Long distance to the hospital.
Lack of transport or ambulance services.
Poor roads or traffic.
Referral coordination problems.
Inability to afford transport.

blocks.text: The woman reaches a facility but does not receive timely, appropriate care.
Examples

items.text: Delayed triage or diagnosis.
Lack of blood products.
Unavailable theatre or anaesthesia services.
Delayed antibiotics or anticonvulsants.
Inadequate monitoring.
Failure to escalate to senior clinicians.

blocks.text: OSCE pearl: More than one delay may contribute to the same death. Avoid attributing the outcome to the woman or her family without examining access barriers and the health system.
A 29-year-old woman delivers vaginally. She develops heavy bleeding after delivery. Her condition deteriorates, and she dies despite resuscitation.
The examiner asks: How would you review this case?

items.text: Time of delivery.
Time bleeding was first noticed.
Estimated or measured blood loss.
Initial pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and mental state.
Time postpartum haemorrhage was diagnosed.
Time uterine massage and uterotonics were initiated.
Time intravenous access, fluids, blood tests and blood products were arranged.
Time tranexamic acid was administered, if indicated.
Time senior obstetric, anaesthetic and theatre teams were called.
Time definitive haemorrhage control was achieved or attempted.
Response to treatment and progression to shock or organ dysfunction.

blocks.text: Use the 4 Ts.

rows: Cervical, vaginal or perineal lacerations; uterine rupture

items.text: Was haemorrhage recognised promptly?
Was the blood loss assessed accurately?
Was the emergency protocol activated?
Were uterotonics and tranexamic acid used appropriately?
Were blood products available and administered without avoidable delay?
Was definitive management, including surgical intervention when necessary, timely?
Were senior staff called early?
Were observations documented and reviewed frequently?
Were communication and handover effective?
Regular postpartum haemorrhage simulation drills.
A standardised haemorrhage trolley or emergency kit.
Clear escalation criteria.
Improved blood bank communication and emergency-release procedures.
Regular review of response times.
Adequate staffing and theatre readiness.
Auditing adherence to the local postpartum haemorrhage protocol.

blocks.text: These are potential interventions, not automatic conclusions. Recommendations should be based on evidence from the actual case.
A woman with severe pre-eclampsia develops seizures and later dies.

items.text: Whether hypertension and severe features were recognised.
Whether blood pressure was monitored appropriately.
Whether magnesium sulfate was administered when indicated.
Whether severe hypertension was treated promptly.
Whether maternal observations and toxicity monitoring were appropriate.
Whether airway support and seizure management were adequate.
Whether senior obstetric and anaesthetic support was obtained.
Whether the timing of delivery and subsequent critical care were appropriate.
Whether referral, transport or equipment shortages contributed.

blocks.text: Potential improvement measures include better use of severe hypertension protocols, magnesium sulfate availability, staff training, early escalation and reliable monitoring systems.
Near-miss reviews are particularly useful because the woman survives and her clinical course can provide detailed lessons about effective and ineffective care.

items.text: Identify weaknesses before they lead to a death.
Understand how timely interventions prevented death.
Improve emergency response systems.
Assess the availability of blood, theatre, critical care and essential medications.
Learn from both successful actions and missed opportunities.

blocks.text: Depending on the adopted WHO or national framework, reviews may use evidence of life-threatening organ dysfunction, such as:

items.text: Cardiovascular dysfunction or shock requiring major resuscitative support.
Respiratory failure requiring advanced support.
Renal dysfunction.
Coagulation or haematological dysfunction.
Neurological dysfunction, including prolonged unconsciousness or stroke.
Hepatic dysfunction associated with severe disease.

blocks.text: The exact criteria and thresholds should follow the specific surveillance or audit protocol being used. Admission to intensive care alone does not automatically establish a WHO maternal near-miss.
Common indicators include:
\[ \text{Maternal near-miss ratio} = \frac{\text{Number of maternal near-miss cases}} {\text{Number of live births}} \times 1{,}000 \]
\[ \text{Maternal mortality ratio} = \frac{\text{Maternal deaths}} {\text{Number of live births}} \times 100{,}000 \]
The denominator and reporting period must be consistent when comparing facilities or time periods.
Another useful measure is the mortality index:
\[ \text{Mortality index} = \frac{\text{Maternal deaths}} {\text{Maternal deaths + near-miss cases}} \times 100\% \]
A higher mortality index among women with life-threatening complications may indicate poorer outcomes, but comparisons must account for case severity, referral patterns and data quality.
Maternal death review is a sensitive professional activity.

items.text: Treat the woman and her family with dignity.
Maintain confidentiality and restrict access to records to authorised personnel.
Follow applicable reporting and documentation requirements.
Use a respectful, factual, non-accusatory approach during review meetings.
Avoid speculation, gossip and disclosure of identifiable details outside authorised settings.
Document findings and recommendations accurately.
Preserve relevant records according to institutional policy.
Communicate appropriately with the family, following local law and hospital policy.

blocks.text: Important distinction: A learning-oriented, non-punitive review does not remove professional accountability. Evidence of misconduct or serious unsafe practice must be handled through the appropriate governance and legal processes.
Root cause analysis is a structured approach to understanding why an adverse event occurred and how the system can be improved.
Problem: Blood transfusion was delayed during a postpartum haemorrhage.

items.text: Why was transfusion delayed? The blood was not ready.
Why was the blood not ready? The blood bank was informed late.
Why was the blood bank informed late? The escalation pathway was unclear.
Why was the escalation pathway unclear? The emergency protocol did not specify responsibility for activation.
What can be changed? Define the activation process, assign responsibility and test the revised system through simulation.

blocks.text: The aim is not simply to identify an individual who made an error, but to determine why the process allowed the error or delay to occur.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. How to present findings at the review meeting

blocks.text: A structured presentation may follow this format:
1. Case summary: Relevant demographic, obstetric and medical history.
2. Clinical course: Chronological timeline from presentation to death or survival.
3. Cause of death or severe morbidity: Immediate, underlying and contributing conditions.
4. Standard of care: What should have occurred according to the applicable protocol.
5. Care actually delivered: What was documented, including timing and response.
6. Contributing factors: Patient, community, referral, staffing, equipment, communication and clinical-management factors.
7. Avoidability: Whether earlier or different care might reasonably have altered the outcome, recognising uncertainty.
8. Recommendations: Specific corrective actions, accountable leads, deadlines and measures of success.
9. Follow-up: How implementation and effectiveness will be assessed.
Avoid declaring a death “definitely preventable” or “unavoidable” without adequate evidence and a structured assessment.

subsections.subsection_title: 13. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the difference between direct and indirect maternal death?

A direct maternal death results from obstetric complications or their management. An indirect maternal death results from a non-obstetric disease that is aggravated by pregnancy or its physiological effects.
Q2. What is the main purpose of maternal death review?
To understand the clinical and system factors contributing to a death and implement changes that prevent similar deaths.
Q3. What are the three delays?
Delay in deciding to seek care, delay in reaching a suitable facility, and delay in receiving adequate care after arrival.
Q4. Is every maternal death preventable?
No. The review should objectively assess avoidable factors and opportunities for improvement. Some deaths may occur despite appropriate care, while others involve preventable delays or deficiencies.
Q5. What is an obstetric near-miss?
A woman who nearly died but survived a life-threatening complication during pregnancy, childbirth or within 42 days after the end of pregnancy.
Q6. Why are near-miss reviews valuable?
They provide opportunities to study severe complications and identify weaknesses or successful interventions without the additional difficulty of reconstructing a fatal outcome.
Q7. What is root cause analysis?
A structured method for identifying underlying system and process factors that contributed to an adverse event, then designing corrective actions.
Q8. Should the review blame the doctor responsible for the case?

The initial review should be factual, fair and focused on learning and system improvement. Where evidence suggests misconduct or serious unsafe practice, the appropriate accountability process should be followed separately.
Q9. What makes a recommendation effective?
It is specific, feasible, measurable, assigned to a responsible person or team, given a deadline and reviewed to determine whether it was implemented and effective.
Q10. What is the maternal mortality ratio?
The number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births in a specified period.

items.text: Confusing maternal mortality ratio with maternal mortality rate.
Confusing a maternal death with a late maternal death.
Focusing only on the final clinical diagnosis without reviewing delays.
Assuming all adverse outcomes are caused by individual negligence.
Failing to reconstruct the clinical timeline.
Recommending vague actions such as “improve care” without measurable targets.
Ignoring referral systems, blood availability, staffing and equipment.
Treating intensive care admission alone as sufficient proof of a maternal near-miss.
Failing to follow up on audit recommendations.
Breaching confidentiality during case discussions.

blocks.text: Reconstruct the timeline
Establish what happened and when.
Establish the cause
Identify underlying and immediate causes.
Verify the standard of care
Compare documented care with applicable guidelines.
Identify delays and deficiencies
Include all three delays and system barriers.
Execute corrective actions
Assign responsibilities and deadlines.
Watch the outcomes
Monitor implementation and re-audit.

Final OSCE takeaway: A strong maternal death review does not stop at identifying what killed the woman. It investigates why the fatal sequence occurred, identifies opportunities for prevention, and ensures that specific changes are implemented and evaluated.
